claim: PD-L1 and its receptor PD-1 are critical regulators of autoimmune, antiviral and antitumoural T cell responses.
source: PD-L1 and its receptor PD-1 are critical regulators of autoimmune, antiviral and antitumoural T cell responses.
evidence: This is a general statement about the established role of PD-L1 and PD-1 in immune regulation, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: The source and biological activity of soluble PD-L1 (sPD-L1) remain incompletely understood.
source: Although the function of its predominant membrane-bound form is well established, the source and biological activity of soluble PD-L1 (sPD-L1) remain incompletely understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge about sPD-L1, based on the state of the field.

claim: sPD-L1 in human healthy tissues and tumours is produced by exaptation of an intronic LINE-2A (L2A) endogenous retroelement in the CD274 gene.
source: Here, we show that sPD-L1 in human healthy tissues and tumours is produced by exaptation of an intronic LINE-2A (L2A) endogenous retroelement in the CD274 gene, encoding PD-L1, which causes omission of the transmembrane domain and the regulatory sequence in the canonical 3' untranslated region.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The L2A exaptation causes omission of the transmembrane domain and the regulatory sequence in the canonical 3' untranslated region.
source: Here, we show that sPD-L1 in human healthy tissues and tumours is produced by exaptation of an intronic LINE-2A (L2A) endogenous retroelement in the CD274 gene, encoding PD-L1, which causes omission of the transmembrane domain and the regulatory sequence in the canonical 3' untranslated region.
evidence: This describes the molecular mechanism by which L2A exaptation affects the CD274 transcript, supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: The alternatively spliced CD274-L2A transcript forms the major source of sPD-L1.
source: The alternatively spliced CD274-L2A transcript forms the major source of sPD-L1 and is highly conserved in hominids, but lost in mice and a few related species.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expression data comparing different CD274 variants.

claim: CD274-L2A is highly conserved in hominids.
source: The alternatively spliced CD274-L2A transcript forms the major source of sPD-L1 and is highly conserved in hominids, but lost in mice and a few related species.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics data presented in Figure 2.

claim: CD274-L2A is lost in mice and a few related species.
source: The alternatively spliced CD274-L2A transcript forms the major source of sPD-L1 and is highly conserved in hominids, but lost in mice and a few related species.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics and expression data showing absence of CD274-L2A in rodents.

claim: CD274-L2A-encoded sPD-L1 lacks measurable T cell inhibitory activity.
source: Importantly, CD274-L2A-encoded sPD-L1 lacks measurable T cell inhibitory activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple T cell suppression assays presented in Figure 4.

claim: CD274-L2A-encoded sPD-L1 functions as a receptor antagonist, blocking the inhibitory activity of PD-L1 bound on cellular or exosomal membranes.
source: Instead, it functions as a receptor antagonist, blocking the inhibitory activity of PD-L1 bound on cellular or exosomal membranes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by antagonism assays presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: PD-1 is induced in T cells proportionally to the strength of T cell receptor (TCR) stimulation.
source: PD-1 is induced in T cells proportionally to the strength of T cell receptor (TCR) stimulation, rendering them receptive to signals from its two ligands, PD-1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and 2 (PD-L2), both of which are membrane-bound proteins (Chamoto et al., 2017; Sharpe and Pauken, 2018; Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PD-L1 and PD-L2 are both membrane-bound proteins.
source: PD-1 is induced in T cells proportionally to the strength of T cell receptor (TCR) stimulation, rendering them receptive to signals from its two ligands, PD-1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and 2 (PD-L2), both of which are membrane-bound proteins (Chamoto et al., 2017; Sharpe and Pauken, 2018; Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PD-1 ligands, supported by citations.

claim: A soluble form of PD-L1 (sPD-L1) has long been documented in healthy human serum.
source: In addition to its major membrane-bound form, a soluble form of PD-L1 (sPD-L1) has long been documented in healthy human serum and found elevated in autoimmune disease and in cancer (Chen et al., 2011; Frigola et al., 2011; Koukourakis et al., 2018; Okuma et al., 2017; Rossille et al., 2014; Wan et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017; Zhu and Lang, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: sPD-L1 is found elevated in autoimmune disease and in cancer.
source: In addition to its major membrane-bound form, a soluble form of PD-L1 (sPD-L1) has long been documented in healthy human serum and found elevated in autoimmune disease and in cancer (Chen et al., 2011; Frigola et al., 2011; Koukourakis et al., 2018; Okuma et al., 2017; Rossille et al., 2014; Wan et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017; Zhu and Lang, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Cell-free PD-L1 is found in exosomes, where it is still membrane-bound.
source: Cell-free PD-L1 is also found in exosomes, where it is still membrane-bound (Chen et al., 2018; Poggio et al., 2019; Ricklefs et al., 2018) and this exosomal PD-L1 (exPD-L1) has confounded detection of membrane-free sPD-L1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Exosomal PD-L1 (exPD-L1) has confounded detection of membrane-free sPD-L1.
source: Cell-free PD-L1 is also found in exosomes, where it is still membrane-bound (Chen et al., 2018; Poggio et al., 2019; Ricklefs et al., 2018) and this exosomal PD-L1 (exPD-L1) has confounded detection of membrane-free sPD-L1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of exosomal PD-L1 and its potential to interfere with detection methods.

claim: Membrane-free non-exosomal sPD-L1 has been demonstrated as a distinct, lower molecular weight, form of PD-L1.
source: Nevertheless, membrane-free non-exosomal sPD-L1 has been demonstrated as a distinct, lower molecular weight, form of PD-L1 (Chen et al., 2011; Frigola et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage and release of the extracellular domain of PD-L1 has been considered as one possible source of sPD-L1, implicating matrix metalloproteinase activity.
source: Proteolytic cleavage and release of the extracellular domain of PD-L1 has been considered as one possible source of sPD-L1, implicating matrix metalloproteinase activity (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: Membrane-free forms of sPD-L1 may be produced by alternative splicing of the CD274 transcript.
source: Membrane-free forms of sPD-L1 may also be produced by alternative splicing of the CD274 transcript (encoding PD-L1).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous observations, supported by subsequent citations.

claim: At least two distinct types of splicing events have been described to remove or affect the exon encoding the PD-L1 transmembrane domain.
source: At least two distinct types of splicing events have been described in several recent reports to remove or affect the exon encoding the PD-L1 transmembrane domain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent reports.

claim: One type of splicing event involves mid-exon splicing.
source: The first involves mid-exon splicing (Gong et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2017), whereas the second is created by alternative polyadenylation (Hassounah et al., 2019; Mahoney et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Another type of splicing event is created by alternative polyadenylation.
source: The first involves mid-exon splicing (Gong et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2017), whereas the second is created by alternative polyadenylation (Hassounah et al., 2019; Mahoney et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The balance between the various CD274 isoforms and their relative contribution to the pool of sPD-L1 remain unknown.
source: However, the balance between the various CD274 isoforms and, consequently, their relative contribution to the pool of sPD-L1 remain unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The biological activity of sPD-L1 is unclear.
source: Also unclear is the biological activity of sPD-L1 (Zhu and Lang, 2017).
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Serum levels of sPD-L1 have been negatively associated with overall survival or response to immunotherapy in diverse cancer types.
source: Serum levels of sPD-L1 have been negatively associated with overall survival or response to immunotherapy in diverse cancer types, including renal cell carcinoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, multiple myeloma, melanoma, and lung cancer (Frigola et al., 2012; Frigola et al., 2011; Koukourakis et al., 2018; Okuma et al., 2017; Rossille et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017), suggesting a possible inhibitory effect.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous clinical studies.

claim: Immune suppression mediated by cell-free PD-L1 has been attributed to exPD-L1 in melanoma, glioblastoma, and mouse models.
source: However, immune suppression mediated by cell-free PD-L1, as well as its negative association with overall survival and response to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy has recently been attributed to exPD-L1 in melanoma, glioblastoma, and mouse models (Chen et al., 2018; Poggio et al., 2019; Ricklefs et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: A study of melanoma patients did not support an inhibitory role for membrane-free sPD-L1.
source: In contrast, a study of melanoma patients did not support an inhibitory role for membrane-free sPD-L1 (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Several studies have reported that sPD-L1 suppresses T cell activation in direct in vitro assays.
source: Several studies have reported that, in direct in vitro assays, sPD-L1 suppresses T cell activation (Frigola et al., 2011; Hassounah et al., 2019; Mahoney et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2017), suggesting it retains the inhibitory activity of the membrane-bound form.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: sPD-L1 completely lacked inhibitory activity in similar in vitro assays in other reports.
source: However, sPD-L1 completely lacked inhibitory activity in similar in vitro assays in other reports (Chen et al., 2018; Gong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The biological activity of sPD-L1 has not yet been established.
source: Thus, despite its potential importance, the biological activity of sPD-L1 has not yet been established.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on conflicting reports in the literature.

claim: Abundant genomic integrations of EREs can generate alternative transcript isoforms through the supply of alternative promoters, splicing, or polyadenylation sites.
source: Abundant genomic integrations of EREs, including long and short interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs and SINEs, respectively) and endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) (Lander et al., 2001) can generate alternative transcript isoforms through the supply of alternative promoters, splicing, or polyadenylation sites (Babaian and Mager, 2016; Burns and Boeke, 2012; Feschotte and Gilbert, 2012; Kassiotis and Stoye, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about EREs, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Exonisation of an intronic germline LINE integration in the CD274 gene is responsible for alternative polyadenylation of a truncated CD274 mRNA.
source: Here, we describe CD274 isoforms generated by transcriptional inclusion of EREs. We show that exonisation of an intronic germline LINE integration in the CD274 gene is responsible for alternative polyadenylation of a truncated CD274 mRNA and for production of sPD-L1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Exonisation of an intronic germline LINE integration in the CD274 gene is responsible for production of sPD-L1.
source: Here, we describe CD274 isoforms generated by transcriptional inclusion of EREs. We show that exonisation of an intronic germline LINE integration in the CD274 gene is responsible for alternative polyadenylation of a truncated CD274 mRNA and for production of sPD-L1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: sPD-L1 produced by LINE exaptation is evolutionarily conserved in humans.
source: We provide further evidence that sPD-L1, produced by LINE exaptation, is evolutionarily conserved in humans, lacks inhibitory activity and is, in fact, a receptor antagonist.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: sPD-L1 produced by LINE exaptation lacks inhibitory activity.
source: We provide further evidence that sPD-L1, produced by LINE exaptation, is evolutionarily conserved in humans, lacks inhibitory activity and is, in fact, a receptor antagonist.
evidence: This is supported by T cell suppression assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: sPD-L1 produced by LINE exaptation is a receptor antagonist.
source: We provide further evidence that sPD-L1, produced by LINE exaptation, is evolutionarily conserved in humans, lacks inhibitory activity and is, in fact, a receptor antagonist.
evidence: This is supported by antagonism assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: The CD274 locus comprises four currently RefSeq or GENCODE annotated variants.
source: Together with numerous retroelements (Figure 1A), the CD274 locus comprises four currently RefSeq or GENCODE annotated variants (Figure 1B; variants 1–4) and two recently cloned variants (Zhou et al., 2017), each generated by one of the two variant 3 splicing alternatives (Figure 1C; variants 9 and 12).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1B and annotation databases.

claim: Three CD274 variants use a terminal ERE instead of the canonical termination and polyadenylation site.
source: Inspection of our recent assembly (Attig et al., 2019) for ERE-overlapping transcripts at this locus identified three variants that use a terminal ERE instead of the canonical termination and polyadenylation site, referred to here as CD274-MIRB, CD274-FLAM_A and CD274-L2A, according to the superfamily of their respective ERE (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the transcript assembly analysis, supported by Figure 1D.

claim: Transcript CD274-MIRB omits the splice site at the end of the canonical exon 6 and terminates at a MIRB SINE integrated in intron 6.
source: Transcript CD274-MIRB omits the splice site at the end of the canonical exon 6 and terminates at a MIRB SINE integrated in intron 6 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the structure of CD274-MIRB, supported by Figure 1D.

claim: Transcript CD274-FLAM_A skips the canonical terminal exon 7 and uses an alternative splice acceptor site at a downstream FLAM_A SINE.
source: Transcript CD274-FLAM_A skips the canonical terminal exon 7 and instead uses an alternative splice acceptor site at a downstream FLAM_A SINE (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the structure of CD274-FLAM_A, supported by Figure 1D.

claim: Transcript CD274-L2A corresponds to CD274 splice variant 4 (NCBI accession NM_001314029).
source: Transcript CD274-L2A corresponds to CD274 splice variant 4 (NCBI accession NM_001314029).
evidence: This links the identified transcript to an existing database entry.

claim: CD274 variant 1 expression was detected in a variety of healthy tissues and was further upregulated in multiple cancers.
source: Expression of CD274 variant 1, encoding the canonical full-length PD-L1, was detected in a variety of healthy tissues and was further upregulated in multiple cancers (Figure 1F), as expected (Sharpe and Pauken, 2018; Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by expression data in Figure 1F and citations to previous literature.

claim: CD274-MIRB and CD274-FLAM_A were expressed at high levels only in a few patient samples.
source: In contrast, CD274-MIRB and CD274-FLAM_A were expressed at high levels only in a few patient samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by expression data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: CD274-MIRB and CD274-FLAM_A transcripts likely arise from processes specific to individual tumours.
source: Although no structural variations that could account for the CD274-MIRB and CD274-FLAM_A transcript structures were found in the highest expressing samples, it is likely that these transcripts arise from processes specific to the individual tumours and indicate the sensitivity of our assembly in capturing transcripts expressed in only a few individuals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sporadic expression pattern and absence of structural variations.

claim: Variant CD274-L2A was readily detected in a variety of healthy tissues and cancer samples.
source: Consistent with two recent reports (Hassounah et al., 2019; Mahoney et al., 2019), variant CD274-L2A was readily detected in a variety of healthy tissues and cancer samples (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by expression data in Figure 1G and citations to recent reports.

claim: CD274-L2A was upregulated in multiple cancers.
source: Similarly to variant 1, CD274-L2A was upregulated in multiple cancers, although levels of CD274-L2A expression levels remained overall 10 times lower than of variant 1 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by expression data in Figure 1G.

claim: Levels of CD274-L2A expression remained overall 10 times lower than variant 1.
source: Similarly to variant 1, CD274-L2A was upregulated in multiple cancers, although levels of CD274-L2A expression levels remained overall 10 times lower than of variant 1 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by expression data in Figure 1G.

claim: Variants 3, 9, and 12 encode truncated forms of PD-L1 lacking the transmembrane domain.
source: In addition to CD274-L2A, variants 3, 9, and 12 also encode truncated forms of PD-L1 lacking the transmembrane domain, due to shared mid-exon splicing events (Gong et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2017) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C and citations to previous studies.

claim: Transcripts corresponding to variants 9 and 12 were neither present in the assembly nor supported by manual splice junction analysis.
source: Transcripts corresponding to variants 9 and 12 were neither present in our assembly nor were they supported by manual splice junction analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the absence of these transcripts in the assembly and splice junction data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Variants 9 and 12 were sporadically expressed in the sample collection.
source: These observations suggest that, similarly to CD274-MIRB and CD274-FLAM_A, variants 9 and 12 were sporadically expressed in our sample collection or in independent cohorts (Gong et al., 2019) and that CD274-L2A is the predominant sPD-L1-encoding variant in the majority of tumour and healthy samples.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of these transcripts in the assembly and their sporadic detection in other cohorts.

claim: CD274-L2A is the predominant sPD-L1-encoding variant in the majority of tumour and healthy samples.
source: These observations suggest that, similarly to CD274-MIRB and CD274-FLAM_A, variants 9 and 12 were sporadically expressed in our sample collection or in independent cohorts (Gong et al., 2019) and that CD274-L2A is the predominant sPD-L1-encoding variant in the majority of tumour and healthy samples.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the expression patterns of different CD274 variants.

claim: sPD-L1 has not been described in laboratory mice.
source: Since sPD-L1 has not been described in laboratory mice and was not detectable in murine cells lines that readily express membrane bound PD-L1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), we first considered the possibility that generation of the CD274-L2A transcript is specific to humans and related species.
evidence: This is supported by the absence of sPD-L1 detection in murine cell lines as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: sPD-L1 was not detectable in murine cell lines that readily express membrane bound PD-L1.
source: Since sPD-L1 has not been described in laboratory mice and was not detectable in murine cells lines that readily express membrane bound PD-L1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), we first considered the possibility that generation of the CD274-L2A transcript is specific to humans and related species.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: No L2A integration is annotated by RepeatMasker in intron 4 of the murine Cd274 gene.
source: Although no L2A integration is annotated by RepeatMasker (www.repeatmasker.org) in intron 4 of the murine Cd274 gene, the major expansion of L2A elements in mammalian genomes is thought to have preceded placental mammal diversification and has now ceased (Goodier and Kazazian, 2008).
evidence: This is based on RepeatMasker annotation and cited literature on L2A expansion.

claim: The major expansion of L2A elements in mammalian genomes preceded placental mammal diversification and has now ceased.
source: Although no L2A integration is annotated by RepeatMasker (www.repeatmasker.org) in intron 4 of the murine Cd274 gene, the major expansion of L2A elements in mammalian genomes is thought to have preceded placental mammal diversification and has now ceased (Goodier and Kazazian, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about L2A evolution, supported by citation.

claim: Comparative genomics revealed surprisingly good alignment of the intronic region across all mammals.
source: Comparative genomics revealed surprisingly good alignment of this intronic region across all mammals (Figure 2A,B), providing evidence for an ancestral L2A integration.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics data in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The good alignment across mammals provides evidence for an ancestral L2A integration.
source: Comparative genomics revealed surprisingly good alignment of this intronic region across all mammals (Figure 2A,B), providing evidence for an ancestral L2A integration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative genomics data.

claim: The alignment was disrupted by a few insertions and deletions in distinct species.
source: This alignment was disrupted by a few insertions and deletions in distinct species (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics data in Figure 2B–E.

claim: The largest insertion was caused by a secondary SINE integration within the L2A integration specific to the porcine Cd274 gene.
source: The largest insertion was caused by a secondary SINE integration within the L2A integration specific to the porcine Cd274 gene (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics data in Figure 2C.

claim: The SINE insertion in the porcine Cd274 gene did not affect the splice donor site at the end of exon 4 or the L2A polyadenylation signal.
source: This insertion did not affect the splice donor site at the end of exon 4 of the L2A polyadenylation signal (Figure 2C), but instead modified the last 9 of the novel 18-amino acid C-terminal sequence (GNILNVSIKMHLALEVPL).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: The SINE insertion in the porcine Cd274 gene modified the last 9 of the novel 18-amino acid C-terminal sequence.
source: This insertion did not affect the splice donor site at the end of exon 4 of the L2A polyadenylation signal (Figure 2C), but instead modified the last 9 of the novel 18-amino acid C-terminal sequence (GNILNVSIKMHLALEVPL).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: In the leporine Cd274 gene, a smaller insertion disrupted the L2A polyadenylation signal.
source: In the leporine Cd274 gene, a smaller insertion disrupted the L2A polyadenylation signal (Figure 2D), which likely compromises mRNA stability.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: The disruption of the L2A polyadenylation signal in the leporine Cd274 gene likely compromises mRNA stability.
source: In the leporine Cd274 gene, a smaller insertion disrupted the L2A polyadenylation signal (Figure 2D), which likely compromises mRNA stability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of polyadenylation signals in mRNA stability.

claim: The Cd274 gene in mice, rats, and hamsters exhibited a 24-nucleotide deletion in the intronic region.
source: Of note, the Cd274 gene in mice, rats, and hamsters exhibited a 24-nucleotide deletion in this intronic region, as well as numerous substitutions (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics data in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The splice donor site at the end of the human CD274 exon 4 is predicted to be a weak motif (GUAAUA).
source: Firstly, in contrast to the splice donor site at the end of the human CD274 exon 4, which is predicted to be a weak motif (GUAAUA), the equivalent splice donor site in the murine Cd274 gene (GUGAGU) was identical to the intronic part of the consensus splice donor motif GUPuAGU (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison to consensus splice motifs, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The splice donor site in the murine Cd274 gene (GUGAGU) was identical to the intronic part of the consensus splice donor motif GUPuAGU.
source: Firstly, in contrast to the splice donor site at the end of the human CD274 exon 4, which is predicted to be a weak motif (GUAAUA), the equivalent splice donor site in the murine Cd274 gene (GUGAGU) was identical to the intronic part of the consensus splice donor motif GUPuAGU (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison to consensus splice motifs, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The polyadenylation signal in the murine L2A integration was mutated and no longer appeared functional.
source: Secondly, the polyadenylation signal in the murine L2A integration was mutated and no longer appeared functional (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Humans, non-human primates and other species, but not rabbits or rodents, have retained the properties required to produce the CD274-L2A transcript.
source: Therefore, humans, non-human primates and other species, but not rabbits or rodents, such as mice, rats and hamsters, have retained the properties required to produce the CD274-L2A transcript.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparative genomics analysis.

claim: CD274-L2A transcripts were detected by qRT-PCR in non-human primate cells.
source: Accordingly, CD274-L2A transcripts were detected by qRT-PCR in non-human primate cells, but not in cells of rabbit or mouse origin, despite expression of the full-length CD274 in all these cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: CD274-L2A transcripts were not detected in cells of rabbit or mouse origin.
source: Accordingly, CD274-L2A transcripts were detected by qRT-PCR in non-human primate cells, but not in cells of rabbit or mouse origin, despite expression of the full-length CD274 in all these cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The ability to produce the CD274-L2A transcript has been selected for, likely through an important biological function.
source: Together with the high degree of conservation in the hominid lineage, these observations suggest that the ability to produce the CD274-L2A transcript has been selected for, likely through an important biological function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evolutionary conservation patterns observed.

claim: The ancestral L2A integration was better preserved in hominids than in rodents.
source: The ancestral L2A integration was better preserved in hominids than in rodents, as suggested by greater sequence homology of the human and chimpanzee L2A integration (67.1%) with the consensus L2A than either the rat or mouse L2A integrations (49.4% and 45.7%, respectively) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by sequence homology analysis in Figure 2F.

claim: The difference in L2A preservation was likely caused by faster evolution of the rodent L2A integration.
source: This difference was likely caused by faster evolution of the rodent L2A integration, as the human L2A integration in the CD274 intron 4 appeared to evolve overall at a similar rate as the average of other L2A integrations of comparable size in the human genome (divergence: 30.3%; deletions: 7.3%; insertions: 0.0% for the CD274 intron 4 L2A integration, and divergence: 27.3%; deletions: 7.8%; insertions: 5.0% for all 437 L2A integrations of 75–77 nucleotides in the human genome).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of divergence rates.

claim: The sequence divergence of the 100 nucleotides between the splice site at the end of CD274 exon 4 and the polyadenylation site in the L2A element was as low as that of coding exons in 10 primate species.
source: Indeed, when the sequence divergence of these 100 nucleotides between the splice site at the end of the CD274 exon 4 and the polyadenylation site in the L2A element was examined in 10 primate species, it was found as low as that of coding exons, contrasting the higher divergence of the rest of CD274 intron 4, other CD274 introns and non-coding exons (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by sequence divergence analysis in Figure 2G.

claim: The low sequence divergence indicates retention of ability to produce CD274-L2A in primates.
source: These findings indicate retention of ability to produce CD274-L2A in primates and certain other species, but its loss through specific mutation in rabbits and rodents.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sequence divergence analysis and comparative genomics.

claim: The ability to produce CD274-L2A was lost through specific mutation in rabbits and rodents.
source: These findings indicate retention of ability to produce CD274-L2A in primates and certain other species, but its loss through specific mutation in rabbits and rodents.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sequence analysis and expression data.

claim: The expression pattern of CD274 variant 1 and CD274-L2A suggested a degree of co-regulation.
source: The expression pattern of the two main CD274 variants, variant 1 and CD274-L2A, suggested a degree of co-regulation (Figure 1G), which was expected given they are both driven by the same promoter.
evidence: This is an observation based on expression data in Figure 1G.

claim: Expression of CD274 variant 1 and CD274-L2A only weakly correlated in healthy tissues (R2 = 0.138).
source: Indeed, expression of the two transcripts only weakly correlated in healthy tissues (R2 = 0.138) or different cancer types (R2 = 0.327) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of CD274 variant 1 and CD274-L2A only weakly correlated in different cancer types (R2 = 0.327).
source: Indeed, expression of the two transcripts only weakly correlated in healthy tissues (R2 = 0.138) or different cancer types (R2 = 0.327) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ratio of CD274-L2A to variant 1 was generally increased in cancer.
source: Importantly, the ratio of CD274-L2A to variant 1 was generally increased in cancer, as exemplified when comparing healthy lung to lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) or lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by expression data in Figure 3A.

claim: Healthy lung samples expressed almost exclusively variant 1, whereas LUAD acquired expression also of CD274-L2A.
source: For example, healthy lung samples expressed almost exclusively variant 1, whereas LUAD acquired expression also of CD274-L2A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by expression data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of CD274 variant 1 and CD274-L2A in 933 cancer cell lines was weakly correlated (R2 = 0.215).
source: Similarly, expression of the two transcripts in 933 cancer cell lines was weakly correlated (R2 = 0.215), with their ratios varying between cell lines by at least two orders of magnitude (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The ratios of CD274 variant 1 to CD274-L2A varied between cell lines by at least two orders of magnitude.
source: Similarly, expression of the two transcripts in 933 cancer cell lines was weakly correlated (R2 = 0.215), with their ratios varying between cell lines by at least two orders of magnitude (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by expression data in Figure 3B.

claim: Both CD274 variant 1 and CD274-L2A were weakly and comparably responsive to IFN-α stimulation.
source: Both variants were weakly and comparably responsive to IFN-α stimulation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression of CD274 variant 1 and CD274-L2A was strongly, but not always equally, responsive to IFN-γ stimulation.
source: Notably, however, expression of the two forms was strongly, but not always equally, responsive to IFN-γ stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3C.

claim: IFN-γ stimulation induced expression predominantly of variant 1 in THP-1 cells and of the CD274-L2A variant in Ramos cells.
source: Indeed, IFN-γ stimulation-induced expression predominantly of variant 1 in THP-1 cells and of the CD274-L2A variant in Ramos cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3C.

claim: Monocytes and neutrophils displayed strongly elevated expression of variant 1 and CD274-L2A following IFN-β treatment of MS patients.
source: Both monocytes and neutrophils displayed strongly elevated expression of variant 1 and CD274-L2A following IFN-β treatment of MS patients, with monocytes expressing the two variants at nearly equal levels (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of CD274-L2A was disproportionately reduced in monocytes and neutrophils isolated from sepsis patients.
source: In contrast, expression of CD274-L2A was disproportionately reduced in monocytes and neutrophils isolated from sepsis patients, in comparison with the same cell types from healthy individuals, whereas expression of variant 1 remained elevated (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The ratio of variant 1 to CD274-L2A was elevated in monocytes and neutrophils from sepsis patients (32 and 34, respectively), in comparison with B cells from the same patients, where it was inverted (0.6).
source: As a result, the ratio of variant 1 to CD274-L2A was elevated in monocytes and neutrophils from sepsis patients (32 and 34, respectively), in comparison with B cells from the same patients, where it was inverted (0.6) (p≤0.004, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: B-3T3.CD274-L2A and HEK293T.CD274-L2A cell lines produced readily detectable levels of sPD-L1 at 10–40 times higher amounts than those detected in supernatants of IFN-γ stimulated HBL-1 cells.
source: Both B-3T3.CD274-L2A and HEK293T.CD274-L2A cell lines produced readily detectable levels of sPD-L1 at 10–40 times higher amounts than those detected by ELISA in supernatants of IFN-γ stimulated HBL-1 cells (Figure 4A; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 4A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Supernatants of IFN-γ stimulated HBL-1 cells contained predominantly exPD-L1.
source: Importantly, supernatants of IFN-γ stimulated HBL-1 cells contained predominantly exPD-L1, production of which was blocked by GW4869, a neutral sphingomyelinase inhibitor that blocks exosome generation, or by siRNA-mediated knockdown of HGS (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), which regulates endosomal transport and exosome formation (Colombo et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2016; Tamai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA and knockdown experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: sPD-L1 produced by HEK293T.CD274-L2A cells was not affected by GW4869 or HGS knockdown.
source: In contrast, sPD-L1 produced by HEK293T.CD274-L2A cells was not affected by these treatments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: sPD-L1 in the supernatant of CD274-L2A-transfected cells migrated close to its theoretical molecular weight of 28 kDa under reducing gel electrophoresis conditions.
source: Moreover, sPD-L1 in the supernatant of CD274-L2A-transfected cells migrated close to its theoretical molecular weight of 28 kDa under reducing gel electrophoresis conditions, but appeared multimerised under native conditions, independently of the type of cell line, in which it was produced (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by gel electrophoresis data in Figure 4B.

claim: sPD-L1 appeared multimerised under native gel electrophoresis conditions.
source: Moreover, sPD-L1 in the supernatant of CD274-L2A-transfected cells migrated close to its theoretical molecular weight of 28 kDa under reducing gel electrophoresis conditions, but appeared multimerised under native conditions, independently of the type of cell line, in which it was produced (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by gel electrophoresis data in Figure 4B.

claim: The multimer of sPD-L1 had a molecular weight consistent with a tetramer.
source: Multimerisation of sPD-L1 seen here is in agreement with recent findings (Mahoney et al., 2019), albeit the multimer in our study had a molecular weight consistent with a tetramer, rather than a dimer.
evidence: This is based on the molecular weight observed in gel electrophoresis, compared to a cited study.

claim: CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1 had no effect on proliferation or granzyme B production of stimulated CD8+ T cells.
source: Under these conditions, no effect of CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1 could be measured on either proliferation or granzyme B (GzmB) production of stimulated CD8+ T cells (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Incubation with HEK293T cells transduced with full-length PD-L1-encoding CD274 variant 1 significantly suppressed CD8+ T cell activation.
source: In contrast, incubation with HEK293T cells transduced with full-length PD-L1-encoding CD274 variant 1 (HEK293T.CD274v1), expectedly and significantly suppressed CD8+ T cell activation (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays in Figure 4C,D.

claim: CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1 produced in B-3T3 cells had no measurable effect on Jurkat T cell expression of CD25 or CD69.
source: Again, CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1 produced in B-3T3 cells had no measureable effect on Jurkat T cell expression of CD25 or CD69 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays in Figure 4E.

claim: Jurkat T cell activation was considerably reduced by addition of conditioned media from HBL-1 cells in a PD-L1-dependent and exosome generation-dependent way.
source: In contrast, Jurkat T cell activation was considerably reduced by addition of conditioned media from HBL-1 cells in a PD-L1-dependent and exosome generation-dependent way (Figure 4E; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays in Figure 4E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Co-culture with HEK293T.CD274v1 displaying membrane-bound PD-L1 significantly reduced activation of Jurkat.PDCD1 cells by CD3 and CD28 stimulation in a PD-L1-dependent manner.
source: Co-culture with HEK293T.CD274v1 displaying membrane-bound PD-L1 significantly reduced activation of Jurkat.PDCD1 cells by CD3 and CD28 stimulation in a PD-L1-dependent manner (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays in Figure 4F.

claim: Incubation of Jurkat.PDCD1 cells with CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1 had no impact on their response to CD3 and CD28 stimulation.
source: Under the same conditions, incubation of Jurkat.PDCD1 cells with CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1 produced in HEK293T cells had no impact on their response to CD3 and CD28 stimulation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays in Figure 4F.

claim: No suppressive activity could be demonstrated for the native CD274-L2A protein product under any of the conditions studied.
source: Therefore, no suppressive activity could be demonstrated for the native CD274-L2A protein product under any of the conditions we have studied.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple T cell suppression assays.

claim: CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1 was able to fully restore responsiveness of primary CD8+ T cells to CD3 and CD28 stimulation when suppressed by membrane-bound PD-L1.
source: Surprisingly, addition of conditioned media from HEK293T.CD274-L2A was also able to fully restore responsiveness of primary CD8+ T cells to CD3 and CD28 stimulation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays in Figure 5A.

claim: CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1 acted as a PD-1 antagonist, blocking the suppressive action of membrane-bound PD-L1 as efficiently as an anti-PD-L1 antibody.
source: These data suggested that CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1 acted as a PD-1 antagonist, blocking the suppressive action of membrane-bound PD-L1 as efficiently as an anti-PD-L1 antibody.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the antagonism assays in Figure 5A.

claim: Addition of CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1 fully restored the response of Jurkat T cells to CD3 and CD28 stimulation in the presence of HBL-1-produced exPD-L1.
source: Again, the addition of CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1, produced in B-3T3 cells fully restored the response of Jurkat T cells to CD3 and CD28 stimulation in the presence of HBL-1-produced exPD-L1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays in Figure 5B.

claim: CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1 restored the response of Jurkat.PDCD1 cells to CD3 and CD28 stimulation suppressed by HBL-1-produced exPD-L1, as efficiently as an anti-PD-L1 antibody.
source: Comparable results were also obtained when HBL-1-produced exPD-L1 was used to suppress the response of Jurkat.PDCD1 cells to CD3 and CD28 stimulation, which again was restored by CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1, produced in HEK293T cells, as efficiently as by an anti-PD-L1 antibody (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays in Figure 5C.

claim: CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1 was able to block the suppression of CD3 and CD28 stimulated Jurkat.PDCD1 cells by membrane-bound PD-L1 provided by HEK293T.CD274v1 cells.
source: Moreover, CD274-L2A-derived sPD-L1, produced in HEK293T cells, was also able to block the suppression of CD3 and CD28 stimulated Jurkat.PDCD1 cells by membrane-bound PD-L1 provided by HEK293T.CD274v1 cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays in Figure 5D.

claim: Co-transfection with CD274-L2A reversed the suppressive effect of CD274v1-derived membrane-bound PD-L1 when HEK293T cells were co-cultured with CD3 and CD28 stimulated Jurkat.PDCD1 cells.
source: Importantly, co-transfection with CD274-L2A reversed the suppressive effect of CD274v1-derived membrane-bound PD-L1 when HEK293T cells were co-cultured with CD3 and CD28 stimulated Jurkat.PDCD1 cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays in Figure 5E.

claim: The CD274-L2A protein product is a natural PD-1 antagonist, which allows T cells to overcome PD-L1-mediated suppression and achieve maximal activation.
source: Collectively, these demonstrate that the CD274-L2A protein product is a natural PD-1 antagonist, which allows T cells to overcome PD-L1-mediated suppression and achieve maximal activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple antagonism assays.

claim: Expression of either murine or human sPD-L1 significantly delayed the growth kinetics of MCA-38 tumours.
source: When subcutaneously transplanted into immunocompetent mice, expression of either murine or human sPD-L1 significantly delayed the growth kinetics of MCA-38 tumours, which was reflected in the tumour masses at the end of the observation period (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by tumour growth data in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The effect of sPD-L1 on tumour growth was comparable to the effect of anti-PD-L1 blockade.
source: This effect on tumour growth was comparable to the effect of anti-PD-L1 blockade (Figure 6A,B), indicating in vivo activity of sPD-L1 as an antagonist of the PD-1 – PD-L1 axis.
evidence: This is supported by tumour growth data in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The effect of sPD-L1 on tumour growth indicates in vivo activity of sPD-L1 as an antagonist of the PD-1 – PD-L1 axis.
source: This effect on tumour growth was comparable to the effect of anti-PD-L1 blockade (Figure 6A,B), indicating in vivo activity of sPD-L1 as an antagonist of the PD-1 – PD-L1 axis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the tumour growth data.

claim: EREs represent a dynamic source of genetic diversity, providing substrates for the evolution of novel host functions, including those of immune genes.
source: EREs represent a dynamic source of genetic diversity, providing substrates for the evolution of novel host functions, including those of immune genes (Burns and Boeke, 2012; Feschotte and Gilbert, 2012; Kassiotis and Stoye, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about EREs, supported by citations.

claim: A HERV integration upstream of the CD5 gene initiates an alternative transcript in healthy B cells that omits the signal peptide-encoding first exon of the canonical transcript.
source: For example, a HERV integration upstream of the CD5 gene initiates an alternative transcript in healthy B cells that omits the signal peptide-encoding first exon of the canonical transcript, resulting in an intracellularly retained form of the otherwise transmembrane CD5 protein (Renaudineau et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an example from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: Exonisation of an intronic L2A element generates a 3' truncated CD274 transcript, omitting the transmembrane domain-encoding sequence and producing secreted sPD-L1.
source: Here, we provided another example where ERE exonisation truncates a transmembrane immune protein, thereby regulating its function. Exonisation of an intronic L2A element generates a 3' truncated CD274 transcript, omitting the transmembrane domain-encoding sequence and producing secreted sPD-L1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: CD274 splice variant 9 and variants 3/12 can produce secreted forms of sPD-L1.
source: Secreted forms of sPD-L1 with both Ig-like domains or only the Ig-like V-type domain intact can also be produced by CD274 splice variant 9 and variants 3/12, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the structure of these variants and their potential to encode soluble forms.

claim: CD274 splice variants 9 and 3/12 were infrequently expressed in the sample collection.
source: However, these variants were infrequently expressed in our sample collection and were also comparably infrequently expressed in independently analysed cohorts (Gong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by expression data and citation to an independent study.

claim: Cell-free forms of PD-L1 were not detected in cells overexpressing exclusively the full-length CD274 transcript.
source: Moreover, cell-free forms of PD-L1 were not detected in cells overexpressing exclusively the full-length CD274 transcript, arguing against proteolytic cleavage as a major source of sPD-L1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no sPD-L1 production from full-length CD274.

claim: These observations indicate CD274-L2A as the predominant source of sPD-L1, at least in the majority of tumour and healthy samples.
source: Together, these observations indicate CD274-L2A as the predominant source of sPD-L1, at least in the majority of tumour and healthy samples.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the expression patterns and absence of other major sources.

claim: The exaptation of L2A element in the generation of sPD-L1 in humans likely extends beyond the provision of an alternative terminal exon.
source: The exaptation of L2A element in the generation of sPD-L1 in humans likely extends beyond the provision of an alternative terminal exon, omitting the transmembrane domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the additional regulatory consequences of L2A exaptation.

claim: CD274-L2A omits the canonical 3' UTR, with important consequences for its regulation.
source: In contrast to all other splice variants that could also produce sPD-L1, CD274-L2A also omits the canonical 3' UTR, with important consequences for its regulation.
evidence: This is based on the structure of CD274-L2A and known regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Binding of tristetraprolin (TTP) to AU-rich elements (ARE) in 3' UTR of the CD274 mRNA decreases its stability, thereby reducing surface PD-L1 expression.
source: Indeed, binding of tristetraprolin (TTP) to AU-rich elements (ARE) in 3' UTR of the CD274 mRNA decreases its stability, thereby reducing surface PD-L1 expression, a mechanism that is counteracted by oncogenic RAS mutations (Coelho et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD274 regulation, supported by citation.

claim: Frequent CD274 3' UTR structural variants found in many cancers cause elevated surface PD-L1 expression in cancer cells.
source: The importance of this regulatory region is also illustrated in frequent CD274 3' UTR structural variants found in many cancers, causing elevated surface PD-L1 expression in cancer cells (Kataoka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Lack of an ARE in CD274-L2A would render it resistant to the destabilising effect of TTP.
source: Lack of an ARE in CD274-L2A, as well as in the other two CD274 variants described here, which use a terminal ERE instead on the canonical 3'UTR, would render them resistant to the destabilising effect of TTP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of ARE in CD274-L2A and known regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Differential post-transcriptional regulation according to the presence of the ARE could explain the often disparate expression of full-length CD274 and CD274-L2A in different types of healthy and transformed cells.
source: Differential post-transcriptional regulation according to the presence of the ARE could, in principle, explain the often disparate expression of full-length CD274 and CD274-L2A in different types of healthy and transformed cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the differential regulation mechanisms.

claim: Differential full-length CD274 and CD274-L2A expression might result from the activity of a specific splicing factor.
source: Alternatively, differential full-length CD274 and CD274-L2A expression might result from the activity of a specific splicing factor, identification of which will require further investigation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis for future investigation.

claim: The critical immune suppressive role for full-length PD-L1, bound on the membrane of cells or exosomes, is amply demonstrated both in animal models and in the success of cancer immunotherapy.
source: The critical immune suppressive role for full-length PD-L1, bound on the membrane of cells or exosomes, is amply demonstrated both in animal models, where genetic deficiency or antibody blockade results in severe phenotypes, and in the success of cancer immunotherapy based on blockade of the PD-L1 – PD-1 interaction (Chamoto et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018; Francisco et al., 2010; Sharpe and Pauken, 2018; Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PD-L1, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Early studies using recombinant sPD-L1 suggested an immune suppressive role either in inhibiting T cell activation or in promoting T cell apoptosis.
source: Early studies using recombinant sPD-L1 suggested an immune suppressive role either in inhibiting T cell activation or in promoting T cell apoptosis (Chinnadurai et al., 2014; Frigola et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: More recent studies using recombinant proteins encoded by CD274-L2A or variants 9 and 3/12 suggested a T cell inhibitory activity for sPD-L1.
source: More recent studies using recombinant proteins encoded by CD274-L2A (Hassounah et al., 2019;Mahoney et al., 2019) or variants 9 and 3/12 (Zhou et al., 2017), also suggested a T cell inhibitory activity for sPD-L1, comparable to or higher than that of the full-length protein.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The reported activity of recombinant sPD-L1 might not reflect that of the natural sPD-L1 protein, but rather of the artificial Fc fusion.
source: However, the reported activity might not reflect that of the natural sPD-L1 protein, but rather of the artificial Fc fusion that was used in the majority of these studies (Chinnadurai et al., 2014; Frigola et al., 2011; Hassounah et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of previous studies, suggesting potential artifacts.

claim: Fusion to Fc is likely to affect the valency of sPD-L1 and may even be presented in a membrane-bound form through binding to Fc receptors.
source: Indeed, fusion to Fc is likely to affect the valency of sPD-L1 and may even be presented in a membrane-bound from through binding to Fc receptors.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of Fc fusions.

claim: At least two reports using the same sPD-L1-Fc fusions found that they can promote, rather than suppress, T cell activation in the presence of APCs.
source: Nevertheless, it is interesting to note that at least two reports using the same sPD-L1-Fc fusions found that they can promote, rather than suppress, T cell activation in the presence of APCs (Steidl et al., 2011; Wan et al., 2006) – an effect that is likely explained by receptor antagonism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human sPD-L1, encoded by CD274-L2A and produced by transfection of murine cells, naturally forms dimers and higher-order multimers.
source: Mahoney et al., recently demonstrated that human sPD-L1, encoded by CD274-L2A and produced by transfection of murine cells, naturally forms dimers and higher-order multimers and that a His-tagged recombinant version, when used at 10–20 µg/ml, can suppress T cell activation in response to CD3 stimulation (Mahoney et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: A His-tagged recombinant version of sPD-L1, when used at 10–20 µg/ml, can suppress T cell activation in response to CD3 stimulation.
source: Mahoney et al., recently demonstrated that human sPD-L1, encoded by CD274-L2A and produced by transfection of murine cells, naturally forms dimers and higher-order multimers and that a His-tagged recombinant version, when used at 10–20 µg/ml, can suppress T cell activation in response to CD3 stimulation (Mahoney et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: No suppression of T cell activation was observed using more physiological concentrations (1–2 ng/ml) of sPD-L1 produced in murine or human cells.
source: Nevertheless, in none of the multiple conditions, we tested did we observe suppression of T cell activation, using more physiological concentrations (1–2 ng/ml) of sPD-L1 produced in murine or human cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: No PD-L1-mediated suppressive activity could be demonstrated by independent studies of cell-free, non-exosomal fractions.
source: Similarly, no PD-L1-mediated suppressive activity could be demonstrated by independent studies of cell-free, non-exosomal fractions (Chen et al., 2018), or of the natural product of CD274 variant 9, even at 2 µg/ml (Gong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to independent studies.

claim: The consensus from these studies is that CD274-L2A-encoded sPD-L1, whilst retaining PD-1 binding activity, lacks suppressive activity.
source: The consensus from these studies is that CD274-L2A-encoded sPD-L1, whilst retaining PD-1 binding activity, lacks suppressive activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current study and cited literature.

claim: The properties of CD274-L2A-encoded sPD-L1 are consistent with a receptor antagonist role.
source: Such properties are consistent with a receptor antagonist role and, indeed, our data clearly demonstrate the ability of CD274-L2A-encoded sPD-L1 to reverse T cell suppression mediated by membrane-bound PD-L1, both cellular and exosomal.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The generation of receptor antagonist sPD-L1 by alternative splicing is at the expense of the canonical transcript encoding the agonist.
source: The generation of receptor antagonist sPD-L1 by alternative splicing is not only at the expense of the canonical transcript encoding the agonist; it additionally offers a means of producing the antagonist without first producing the agonist, as would be the case with proteolytic cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism and consequences of alternative splicing.

claim: Antagonistic activity by sPD-L1 is reminiscent of a growing number of membrane-bound cytokines as well as co-stimulatory or co-inhibitory molecules and their receptors, whose soluble versions assume a blocking or antagonist function.
source: Antagonistic activity by sPD-L1 is reminiscent of a growing number of membrane-bound cytokines as well as co-stimulatory or co-inhibitory molecules and their receptors, whose soluble versions assume a blocking or antagonist function (Bemelmans et al., 2017; Dinarello, 1998; Gu et al., 2018; Guégan and Legembre, 2018; Zhu and Lang, 2017).
evidence: This places the findings in the context of broader biological phenomena, supported by citations.

claim: Many soluble forms of membrane-bound molecules are produced by alternatively spliced mRNAs.
source: Although soluble forms of many of these molecules are thought to be produced by proteolytic cleavage of the membrane-bound forms, many others are produced by alternatively spliced mRNAs (Gu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Soluble PD-1, soluble CTLA-4, and soluble CD80 are all produced by alternative transcript variants that omit their respective transmembrane domain-encoding exons.
source: These include soluble PD-1, soluble CTLA-4, and soluble CD80, all of which are produced by alternative transcript variants that omit their respective transmembrane domain-encoding exons (Kakoulidou et al., 2007; Magistrelli et al., 1999; Nielsen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Generation of soluble forms of several co-inhibitory molecules underscores their broader involvement in immune regulation.
source: Generation of soluble forms of several co-inhibitory molecules underscores their broader involvement in immune regulation, but also the complexity of their interconnected pathways.
evidence: This is an inference about the biological significance of soluble co-inhibitory molecules.

claim: The evolutionary conservation of sPD-L1 production in humans suggests it is an important contributor to the regulation of PD-L1 activity.
source: Whilst certainly not acting alone, the evolutionary conservation of sPD-L1 production in humans suggests it is an important contributor to the regulation of PD-L1 activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evolutionary conservation data.

claim: Membrane-bound PD-L1 can be antagonised by in cis binding to CD80 in human and murine dendritic cells.
source: Membrane-bound PD-L1 can be antagonised also by in cis binding to CD80, both in human and murine dendritic cells (Sugiura et al., 2019), and sPD-1 has long been hypothesised to function as a decoy receptor, reducing availability of membrane-bound PD-L1 (Zhu and Lang, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: sPD-1 has long been hypothesised to function as a decoy receptor, reducing availability of membrane-bound PD-L1.
source: Membrane-bound PD-L1 can be antagonised also by in cis binding to CD80, both in human and murine dendritic cells (Sugiura et al., 2019), and sPD-1 has long been hypothesised to function as a decoy receptor, reducing availability of membrane-bound PD-L1 (Zhu and Lang, 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: sPD-L1 can interfere with the effect of anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy.
source: Moreover, sPD-L1 can interfere with the effect of anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citation to a study showing this effect.

claim: Tumours harbouring mutations in the TDP-43 splicing factor from two non-small cell lung cancer patients overproduce sPD-L1 encoded by CD274 variant 9 or an alternative splice variant omitting exons 5 and 6.
source: Indeed, tumours harbouring mutations in the TDP-43 splicing factor from two non-small cell lung cancer patients have recently been shown to overproduce sPD-L1 encoded by CD274 variant 9 or an alternative splice variant omitting exons 5 and 6, which can act as a decoy for PD-L1-targeting antibodies, thereby reducing the effect of immunotherapy (Gong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: sPD-L1 can act as a decoy for PD-L1-targeting antibodies, thereby reducing the effect of immunotherapy.
source: Indeed, tumours harbouring mutations in the TDP-43 splicing factor from two non-small cell lung cancer patients have recently been shown to overproduce sPD-L1 encoded by CD274 variant 9 or an alternative splice variant omitting exons 5 and 6, which can act as a decoy for PD-L1-targeting antibodies, thereby reducing the effect of immunotherapy (Gong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.
